newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - "Shine" director looks beyond glare of Oscars.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "Shine" director looks beyond glare of Oscars.

text.p: Australian director Scott Hicks is tired.

His film "Shine" is up for seven Oscars at next week's Academy Awards and he has just returned from a three-week promotional tour of the United States, packing interview after interview into 18-hour days.

Back home, hoping for some peace and quiet with his family before flying out on Friday for Hollywood's big night, he has Adelaide fans and critics queueing at his door for a look at the "local boy made good".
"I am not sick of it, I am exhausted by it," he told Reuters of his eight months promoting the film, inspired by pianist David Helfgott's remarkable battle against a mental breakdown.

"But I feel I am coming to the end of a cycle with it, especially I think at the Oscars, and I have to start getting on with other projects which have really been on hold for the whole period, making a decision on what I do next."

"Shine" has tugged at the heartstrings of audiences around the world, packing cinemas and collecting a swag of awards, including nine from the Australian Film Institute and a Golden Globe Best Actor award for star Geoffrey Rush.

It has swept Helfgott to heights of which he never dreamed. The groaning pianist has packed out concert halls in Australia, Britain and the United States and seen his version of Rachmaninoff's Third Concerto top the American classical music charts.

The White House is reported to have booked the low-budget independent film for a Thanksgiving Day screening, and pop superstar Michael Jackson saw the film when his world tour took him to Adelaide, Hicks' hometown in South Australia.
OSCARS ADD TO BOX OFFICE SUCCESS

British bookmakers have "Shine" as second favourite for best picture at the Oscars -- behind the romantic desert epic "The English Patient" -- and have installed Rush as hot favourite to take the statuette for best actor.

Sitting in his new inner-city Adelaide office, provided by a "first-look" deal with Hollywood producer Steven Spielberg, Hicks said success at the Oscars would definitely carry through to the box office.
"But I certainly will not feel like a loser if I do not win," he added, the back wall of his office stacked with some of the 120 scripts sent for his perusal since "Shine".
"I feel I have got to a height in my career that I honestly never anticipated," he said, looking every inch the student film-maker with his long hair, jeans, sneakers and leather jacket.

Under the deal with Spielberg's DreamWorks SKG, Spielberg gets first look at any idea Hicks has or material he controls. Hicks however is free to direct films owned by others, and he is currently working with Warner Bros on bringing Donna Tartt's best-selling novel "The Secret History" to the screen.
HELFGOTT CRITICS OVERSTEP MARK

Hicks, a 44-year-old who was born in Uganda and has lived in Adelaide for 30 years, is already accustomed to being one of the film industry's hot new properties. He handles questions about the impact of "Shine" softly and easily.
But he pulls no punches against the American critics who savaged Helfgott for his patchy, idiosyncratic performances on his current U.S. concert tour.

"It intrigues me how violent their criticisms have been, it has often been quite virulent and often quite personal," Hicks said angrily. "I think sometimes they have overstepped the mark in their criticism of him as a person."
Hicks concedes the controversy may affect the film's chances at the Academy Awards, but he hopes the message and integrity of the film prevail.

"The film is never about... being the best, it was always about the acceptance and finding your place in the world and that is David's triumph; he has been accepted for who is is, with all his flaws, as a person and a pianist," he said.
